title: NASA solicits lunar reactor proposals
html:
NASA has launched a request for proposals seeking industry partners to develop Lunar Reactor-1 (LR-1), a small fission power system that the agency said could support “future habitats, communications systems, rovers, scientific instruments, and other essential infrastructure.”

“This request for proposals represents an important step forward as NASA partners with industry to establish an enduring human presence on the lunar surface,” said Brian Giblin, LR-1 program manager at NASA. “A reliable source of safe and abundant energy will be vital to future exploration of the lunar and Martian surface. Space nuclear systems will provide continuous power to NASA assets in any environment without dependency on sunlight.”

Design requirements: According to NASA’s timeline, the agency expects LR-1 to be launch-ready by December 2030. It should generate 20 kWe and be able to maintain that level of generation after a single failure within the system, ensuring continued delivery of the minimum power demand.

It will use closed Brayton conversion and high-assay low-enrichment uranium, and it must be shielded such that crew members in a habitable zone 1 kilometer from the reactor will receive a maximum of 5 rem above lunar background per year.

LR-1 is expected to be capable of operating continuously and automatically with intermittent communications from Earth for at least five years without maintenance, though if temporary shutdown is needed, it should be able to do that without detriment to performance and should be able to restart.

The reactor should be able to operate under the environmental conditions at the lunar south pole, including at least 14.75 days of continuous darkness. At mission completion, it must be able to be shut down safely and deplete or control all sources of stored energy to enter a “permanent, passive safe state.”

Scope of work: This RFP covers preliminary design and hardware demonstration. Selected contractors are expected “to leverage and advance prior NASA Fission Surface Power projects and studies,” according to the agency.

NASA’s statement of work notes that selected industry partners will have 18 months to complete component-level radiation exposure testing and all hardware demonstrations, including an electrically heated integrated systems test.

It states, “A primary work element of this task is to design, build, and test a nonnuclear Engineering Test Unit (ETU) that incorporates the key subsystem technologies needed for a future LR-1 flight system.”

The ETU should demonstrate, at minimum, reactor heat transport, power conversion, heat rejection, and power management and distribution using full-scale components in a lunar-relevant thermal-vacuum environment.

While the reactor will not be operated at power before landing on the moon, a zero-power critical test prior to launch will be allowed.

LR-1 will be regulated under the Department of Energy’s safety standards, including the DOE-STD-1271 authorization pathway for nuclear facilities. It is managed by NASA’s Space Reactors Division, which is also responsible for Space Reactor-1 (SR-1) Freedom, a nuclear electric propulsion rocket that is scheduled to launch in 2028 and is expected to provide data that can support the development of LR-1.

According to NASA, “While the primary purpose of the request for proposals is to advance the technology, testing, and flight design of LR-1, NASA may issue additional task orders to support the development of other space nuclear power systems.”
